ca.name: California
ca.issuer: The school you attend. Home-schooled, private and charter students go through their own school.
steps: Get the job offer first. Schools usually will not issue a permit until an employer agrees to hire you.
Fill out the Statement of Intent (form B1-1). You, a parent or guardian, and your employer all sign it. Your school has it online or at the counselor or career office.
Turn it in at your school. The school checks it and issues the Permit (form B1-4) with the most hours you may work.
Give the permit to your employer. They keep it on file.
bring: The signed Statement of Intent (form B1-1)
Proof of age, such as a birth certificate
The name and contact of your employer
A parent or guardian to sign
ca.timing: Some districts take a day and some take up to a week. Start one to two weeks before your first shift.
ca.renew: Permits issued during the school year run out soon after the next school year starts, so renew it each year.

links.t: Full California rules on this site

hours.12: School days: no work. Non-school days: up to 8 hours. Only between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. (9 p.m. from June 1 to Labor Day). You need to have finished 7th grade to work while school is in session.
hours.14: School days: up to 3 hours, outside school hours. Non-school days: up to 8 hours. School weeks: up to 18 hours. When school is out: up to 8 hours a day and 40 a week. Only between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. (9 p.m. from June 1 to Labor Day).
hours.16: School days: up to 4 hours. Non-school days: up to 8 hours. Up to 48 hours a week. Between 5 a.m. and 10 p.m. (12:30 a.m. before a non-school day).

ca.wage: $16.90 an hour in 2026 and $17.40 from Jan 1, 2027. Some cities pay more, so ask your employer for the rate.

minAge.note: At 12 and 13 you can do things like babysitting, pet care, yard work and newspaper delivery.

job.text: Almost every worker under 18 needs a Permit to Employ and Work for each paid job at a business, even in summer.

program.text: A paid city or nonprofit youth program is a paid job, so the same permit applies. Many programs tell you what to turn in, so read their instructions and ask which school form they want.

odd.text: Babysitting, lawn mowing, yard work and other occasional odd jobs in private homes do not need a permit.

own.text: Running your own business (tutoring, pet care, selling crafts) does not need a permit. Delivering newspapers on your own route does not either.

volunteer.text: True unpaid volunteering does not need a permit. Have your parent's permission on file with your school (California regulation 5 CCR 10121).

intern.text: An unpaid internship at a nonprofit, school or library is usually fine and is not a paid job, so no work permit. At a for-profit company it is only allowed if you are the one who mainly benefits, like a class. Otherwise it should be a paid job, and then you need the permit.

family.text: Working for your parent's business usually still needs a permit, and the usual age and hour rules apply. The exception is farm or home work on property the parent controls.

acting.text: Acting and modeling use a different permit from the Labor Commissioner, not the school permit. Call 833-526-4636 before you accept.

ca.adult: Graduates of high school and teens with a certificate of proficiency do not need a permit. At 18 you do not need one.

ga.name: Georgia
ga.issuer: Your school (you get a data sheet there), or the county school superintendent's office if you do not go to school.
steps: Line up the job first. Your employer fills in a section about the job.
Get the data sheet from your school, or start online with Georgia DOL.
Bring a certified birth certificate.
Get the school letter saying you are enrolled full time and your attendance is in good standing. It is updated each January.
bring: The data sheet with the employer's section filled in
School letter: enrolled full time, attendance in good standing
ga.timing: Not stated on the pages we read. Ask your school office how long it takes.
ga.renew: Not stated on the pages we read.
ga.call: Georgia DOL Child Labor unit: 1-877-709-8185, childlabor@gdol.ga.gov

links.t: US DOL Fact Sheet 32: youth minimum wage

hours.14: At most employers the federal limits apply, and they are stricter. School days: up to 3 hours. School weeks: up to 18 hours. Non-school days: up to 8 hours. When school is out: up to 40 hours a week. Only between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. (9 p.m. from June 1 to Labor Day).
hours.16: Georgia and federal law set no hour limits at 16 and 17. Dangerous jobs are still off limits, and anyone 17 or younger may not take orders for or serve alcohol, except where it is sold to take off the premises.

ga.wage: $7.25 an hour at nearly every employer. Under federal law an employer may pay $4.25 to workers under 20 for their first 90 days.

minAge.note: Most non-farm jobs covered by federal law start at 14.

job.text: Every minor under 16 needs an Employment Certificate for a paid job. At 16 and 17 it is not required.

program.text: A paid youth program is a paid job, so under 16 you need the Employment Certificate. Ask the program what they want you to turn in.

odd.text: The Georgia pages we read do not say whether odd jobs for neighbors need a certificate. Ask Georgia DOL Child Labor: 1-877-709-8185.

own.text: The Georgia pages we read do not say whether running your own small business needs a certificate. Ask Georgia DOL Child Labor: 1-877-709-8185.

volunteer.text: Volunteering without pay does not need a permit, and a work permit is not required if you are not being paid for community service.

intern.text: We found no Georgia page that sets its own internship rule, so the federal fact sheet is the guide. If the internship is unpaid, a work permit is not required for unpaid community service. If it asks for regular hours and real jobs for free, ask a parent or counselor to check it.

family.text: The Georgia pages we read do not cover work for a parent's business. Ask Georgia DOL Child Labor: 1-877-709-8185.

acting.text: Georgia has its own page for minors in entertainment. Start at dol.georgia.gov/employers/child-labor-and-minors-entertainment and ask Georgia DOL Child Labor: 1-877-709-8185.

ga.adult: At 16 and older you do not need an Employment Certificate in Georgia.

ny.name: New York
ny.issuer: Your school. In New York City you apply at your own school, or at the public high school nearest home if you are not in school.
steps: For a part-time student job you do not need an employer first.
Fill out the application and have a parent sign it.
Bring proof of age, a doctor's note that you are fit to work, and your school ID or a recent report card.
Hand it in at school. Your employer keeps your original papers.
bring: Proof of age, such as a birth certificate with a seal
A doctor's note from the last 12 months (a school sports physical counts)
School ID or a recent report card
ny.timing: Not stated on the pages we read. The state says a new digital process starts in 2027.
ny.renew: Not stated on the pages we read.
ny.call: New York State Department of Labor: 888-469-7365 or 888-525-2267

links.t: New York rules on this site

hours.14: School in session: not before 7 a.m. or after 7 p.m., up to 3 hours on a school day, 8 on a non-school day, 18 a week, 6 days a week. School closed all week: up to 8 hours a day and 40 a week.
hours.16: School in session: up to 4 hours on a day before a school day (Monday to Thursday), 8 hours Friday to Sunday and holidays, 28 a week, 6 days a week. Not before 6 a.m. and generally not after 10 p.m., or midnight with a parent's written permission.

ny.wage: $17.00 an hour in New York City, Long Island and Westchester, and $16.00 in the rest of the state (2026).

minAge.note: Ages 14 to 17 need working papers for any job in New York.

job.text: Ages 14 to 17 need an employment certificate, called working papers, for any job in New York.

program.text: A paid youth program is a job, so ages 14 to 17 need working papers. Many programs, including the NYC summer youth program, tell you what to turn in, so read their steps.

odd.text: Babysitting and casual yard work or chores at home are exempt from working papers.

own.text: The New York pages we read do not say whether your own small business needs working papers. Ask the State Department of Labor: 888-469-7365.

volunteer.text: Unpaid volunteers are allowed at charitable, educational or religious organizations, and they may not replace or add to paid staff. The pages we read do not require working papers for volunteers, so confirm with your school.

intern.text: New York is stricter than most states. A for-profit can have an unpaid intern only if all its criteria are met, including a clear written notice before the internship starts that no wages are paid. For nonprofits there is no intern exemption, only volunteers. If you are unsure, ask the state labor department.

family.text: The New York pages we read do not cover work for a parent's business. Ask the State Department of Labor: 888-469-7365.

acting.text: Child performers have separate rules in New York that we did not read. Ask the State Department of Labor: 888-469-7365.

ny.adult: At 18 you do not need working papers in New York.

il.name: Illinois
il.issuer: A school issuing officer. The Illinois Department of Labor does not issue it. Call your school district or Regional Office of Education first.
steps: Get a letter of intent to hire from the employer naming the job and hours.
You and a parent apply in person, unless your school allows remote.
Bring proof of age, a school schedule statement and a physical-fitness statement.
The school may not charge a fee.
bring: Letter of intent to hire (job and hours)
il.timing: Not stated on the pages we read. Call your school district first.
il.renew: The certificate lasts one year for that employer.
il.call: Illinois Department of Labor child labor questions: 312-793-5570, hotline 800-645-5784

hours.14: No more than 18 hours in a school week, 40 when school is out, 3 hours on a school day, 8 hours in any 24 hours, and only between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. (until 9 p.m. from June 1 to Labor Day). A meal break of at least 30 minutes by the 5th hour in a row.
hours.16: The Illinois child labor law does not limit your hours at 16 and 17, and federal law does not either.

il.wage: $15.00 an hour. Under 18 you may be paid $13.00 for your first 650 hours in a year with one employer. Chicago is $17.05 from July 1, 2026.

minAge.note: Most non-farm jobs covered by federal law start at 14.

job.text: Illinois requires a certificate for workers under 16. It is not required at 16 or 17.

program.text: A paid youth program is a paid job, so under 16 you need the certificate. Programs such as the Chicago summer youth jobs tell you what to turn in, so read their steps.

odd.text: The Illinois pages we read do not say whether odd jobs for neighbors need a certificate. Ask Illinois DOL child labor questions: 312-793-5570.

own.text: The Illinois pages we read do not say whether your own small business needs a certificate. Ask Illinois DOL child labor questions: 312-793-5570.

volunteer.text: The Illinois pages we read do not say whether volunteering needs a certificate. Ask Illinois DOL child labor questions: 312-793-5570.

intern.text: We found no Illinois page that sets its own internship rule, so the federal fact sheet is the guide. If an internship asks you to work regular hours and do real jobs for free, ask a parent or counselor to check it.

family.text: The Illinois pages we read do not cover work for a parent's business. Ask Illinois DOL child labor questions: 312-793-5570.

acting.text: Illinois has separate rules for child performers that we did not read. Ask Illinois DOL child labor questions: 312-793-5570.

il.adult: At 16 and older you do not need a certificate in Illinois.

wa.name: Washington
wa.permit: Parent and school authorization form (the employer holds the Minor Work Permit)
wa.issuer: The employer gets the Minor Work Permit endorsement. You, a parent, your employer and a school official sign the authorization form.
steps: Get the job first. The employer must have a Minor Work Permit endorsement on their business license (the fee is $0).
Fill out the parent and school authorization form, or the parent authorization for summer work form if you are hired only for summer break.
Get the form signed by your employer, you, a school official and your parent or guardian.
Give it to your employer. It expires each Sept 30 and must be renewed every year.
bring: The authorization form with all four signatures
A school official to sign (school year)
wa.timing: Not stated on the pages we read.
wa.renew: The form expires each school year on Sept 30 and must be renewed.

hours.14: School week: up to 3 hours a day (8 on Saturday and Sunday), 16 a week, 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. School out: up to 8 hours a day, 40 a week, 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. (9 p.m. from June 1 to Labor Day).
hours.16: School week: up to 4 hours a day (8 Friday to Sunday), 20 a week, 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. School out: up to 8 hours a day, 48 a week, 5 a.m. to midnight. Generally no work during the hours your neighborhood school is in session.

wa.wage: $17.13 an hour in 2026. Employers may pay 85 percent of that ($14.56) to workers 14 and 15. Seattle's minimum is higher.

minAge.note: In general the minimum age to work in Washington is 14.

job.text: Every minor needs a parent and school authorization form for each paid job at a private employer. Public employers such as state and city governments are not covered by Washington's child labor rules.

program.text: A paid youth program is a paid job, so the job rule applies. Read the program's own steps for what to turn in.

odd.text: The pages we read do not say whether odd jobs for neighbors need a permit. Ask Washington L&I (lni.wa.gov/TeenWorkers).

own.text: The pages we read do not say whether running your own small business needs a permit. Ask Washington L&I (lni.wa.gov/TeenWorkers).

volunteer.text: Washington's child labor rules apply to minor employees, not volunteers. Federal rules still apply.

intern.text: We found no page here that sets its own internship rule, so the federal fact sheet is the guide: a for-profit generally must pay an intern who is really an employee. Ask a parent or school counselor to check an unpaid one at a business, and ask Washington L&I (lni.wa.gov/TeenWorkers).

family.text: The pages we read do not say about work for a parent's business. Ask Washington L&I (lni.wa.gov/TeenWorkers).

acting.text: The pages we read do not say about acting or modeling. Ask Washington L&I (lni.wa.gov/TeenWorkers).

wa.adult: At 18 you do not need a minor work authorization in Washington.

tx.name: Texas
tx.permit: Certificate of Age (optional, some employers ask)
steps: Texas does not require a work permit for teens on the pages we read.
Ask the employer whether they want a Certificate of Age. If they do, get the form from the Texas Workforce Commission.
Have proof of your age ready, such as a birth certificate.
bring: The Certificate of Age form, only if your employer asks
tx.timing: Not stated on the pages we read.
tx.renew: Not stated on the pages we read.
tx.call: Texas Workforce Commission child labor line (twc.texas.gov)

links.t: US DOL Fact Sheet 32: youth minimum wage

hours.14: At most employers the federal limits apply and they are stricter: school days up to 3 hours, school weeks up to 18 hours, non-school days up to 8 hours, 40 a week when school is out, between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. (9 p.m. from June 1 to Labor Day). Texas also says no more than 8 hours a day or 48 a week, nothing before 5 a.m., and nothing past 10 p.m. before a school day.
hours.16: A child who is 16 or 17 has no restrictions on the number of hours or times of day they may work.

tx.wage: $7.25 an hour (Texas follows the federal minimum wage). Under federal law an employer may pay $4.25 to workers under 20 for their first 90 days.

minAge.note: It is illegal to employ a child under 14 in Texas except under specific circumstances.

job.text: The Texas pages we read do not require a work permit for teens. Some employers may ask for a Certificate of Age from the Texas Workforce Commission.

program.text: A paid youth program is a paid job, so the job rule applies. Read the program's own steps for what to turn in.

odd.text: The pages we read do not say whether odd jobs for neighbors need a permit. Ask the Texas Workforce Commission.

own.text: The pages we read do not say whether running your own small business needs a permit. Ask the Texas Workforce Commission.

volunteer.text: The pages we read do not say whether volunteering needs a permit. Ask the Texas Workforce Commission.

intern.text: We found no page here that sets its own internship rule, so the federal fact sheet is the guide: a for-profit generally must pay an intern who is really an employee. Ask a parent or school counselor to check an unpaid one at a business, and ask the Texas Workforce Commission.

family.text: The pages we read do not say about work for a parent's business. Ask the Texas Workforce Commission.

acting.text: The pages we read do not say about acting or modeling. Ask the Texas Workforce Commission.

tx.adult: At 18 you do not need a Certificate of Age.

mn.name: Minnesota
mn.permit: Employment certificate (only for school-day work during school hours)
steps: Minnesota does not require a general work permit on the pages we read.
A minor under 16 needs an employment certificate only to work on school days during school hours.
Keep proof of age ready, such as a birth certificate. Employers keep it in payroll records.
mn.timing: Not stated on the pages we read.
mn.renew: Not stated on the pages we read.
mn.call: Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry (dli.mn.gov/child-labor)

hours.14: At most employers the federal limits apply and they are stricter: school days up to 3 hours, school weeks up to 18 hours, non-school days up to 8 hours, 40 a week when school is out, between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. (9 p.m. from June 1 to Labor Day). Minnesota's own limit for under 16: not before 7 a.m. or after 9 p.m., no more than 8 hours in 24 or 40 a week.
hours.16: High school students 16 and 17 may not work after 11 p.m. on evenings before school days or before 5 a.m. on school days. With written parent permission this moves to 11:30 p.m. and 4:30 a.m.

mn.wage: $11.41 an hour in 2026 and $11.87 from Jan 1, 2027. Minneapolis and Saint Paul have their own higher minimums.

minAge.note: Fourteen is the minimum age of employment in Minnesota, with exceptions such as newspaper carriers at 11.

job.text: Minnesota does not require a general work permit. Under 16 you need an employment certificate only to work on school days during school hours.

program.text: A paid youth program is a paid job, so the job rule applies. Read the program's own steps for what to turn in.

odd.text: The pages we read do not say whether odd jobs for neighbors need a permit. Ask the Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry.

own.text: The pages we read do not say whether running your own small business needs a permit. Ask the Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry.

volunteer.text: The pages we read do not say whether volunteering needs a permit. Ask the Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry.

intern.text: We found no page here that sets its own internship rule, so the federal fact sheet is the guide: a for-profit generally must pay an intern who is really an employee. Ask a parent or school counselor to check an unpaid one at a business, and ask the Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry.

family.text: The pages we read do not say about work for a parent's business. Ask the Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry.

acting.text: The pages we read do not say about acting or modeling. Ask the Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry.

mn.adult: At 18 you have no special youth rules in Minnesota.

wi.name: Wisconsin
wi.permit: Work permit for 14 and 15 year olds
wi.issuer: Your parent or guardian applies and pays for the permit. The employer must reimburse the $10 fee by your first paycheck.
steps: Get the job first.
Your parent or guardian applies for the work permit through the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development.
Give the permit to your employer before you start.
wi.timing: Not stated on the pages we read.
wi.renew: Not stated on the pages we read.

hours.14: School days: up to 3 hours a day and 18 a week. Non-school days: up to 8 hours a day and 40 a week. 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., or 9 p.m. from June 1 to Labor Day.
hours.16: State and federal laws do not limit the hours that minors 16 and older may work, but not during required school attendance.

wi.wage: $7.25 an hour. Employers may pay $5.90 an hour for the first 90 days.

minAge.note: Minors must be at least 14 to be employed in most gainful occupations.

job.text: Most employers hiring minors need a valid work permit for each minor before work starts. The DWD pages disagree on the ages (one says 12 to 15, one says 14 and 15), so confirm with DWD.

program.text: A paid youth program is a paid job, so the job rule applies. Read the program's own steps for what to turn in.

odd.text: The pages we read do not say whether odd jobs for neighbors need a permit. Ask the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development.

own.text: The pages we read do not say whether running your own small business needs a permit. Ask the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development.

volunteer.text: A work permit is not needed for volunteer work for a nonprofit organization, not as an employee.

intern.text: We found no page here that sets its own internship rule, so the federal fact sheet is the guide: a for-profit generally must pay an intern who is really an employee. Ask a parent or school counselor to check an unpaid one at a business, and ask the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development.

family.text: The pages we read do not say about work for a parent's business. Ask the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development.

acting.text: The pages we read do not say about acting or modeling. Ask the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development.

wi.adult: At 16 and older you do not need a work permit in Wisconsin.

in.name: Indiana
in.issuer: Indiana does not issue work permits
steps: Indiana no longer requires work permits for 14 through 17 year olds on the state pages we read.
Ask your employer what proof of age they want.
Check the hour rules for your age below.
bring: Proof of age, if your employer asks
in.timing: Not stated on the pages we read.
in.renew: Not stated on the pages we read.
in.call: Indiana Department of Labor Youth Employment Division: (317) 232-2655

hours.14: School days: up to 3 hours. School weeks: up to 18 hours. Non-school days: up to 8 hours, 40 a week. Not before 7 a.m. or after 7 p.m. (9 p.m. from June 1 to Labor Day). Not during school hours.
hours.16: There are no hour restrictions for 16 and 17 year olds.

in.wage: $7.25 an hour. Employers may pay $4.25 to workers under 20 for the first 90 days.

minAge.note: We did not find an explicit minimum working age on the Indiana pages. The rules are written for 14 to 15 and 16 to 17 year olds, and the federal minimum is 14.

job.text: Indiana no longer requires work permits for ages 14 to 17.

program.text: A paid youth program is a paid job, so the job rule applies. Read the program's own steps for what to turn in.

odd.text: The pages we read do not say whether odd jobs for neighbors need a permit. Ask the Indiana Department of Labor, (317) 232-2655.

own.text: The pages we read do not say whether running your own small business needs a permit. Ask the Indiana Department of Labor, (317) 232-2655.

volunteer.text: The pages we read do not say whether volunteering needs a permit. Ask the Indiana Department of Labor, (317) 232-2655.

intern.text: We found no page here that sets its own internship rule, so the federal fact sheet is the guide: a for-profit generally must pay an intern who is really an employee. Ask a parent or school counselor to check an unpaid one at a business, and ask the Indiana Department of Labor, (317) 232-2655.

family.text: The pages we read do not say about work for a parent's business. Ask the Indiana Department of Labor, (317) 232-2655.

acting.text: The pages we read do not say about acting or modeling. Ask the Indiana Department of Labor, (317) 232-2655.

in.adult: No work permit is needed in Indiana.

mi.name: Michigan
mi.issuer: From Oct 2, 2026 the state's online youth employment permit system, used by the employer and the minor. Local schools no longer issue permits.
steps: Get the job first.
You and your employer complete the permit in the state's online system (YEPP).
Do not start work before the permit is valid.
bring: Your parent or guardian, if the system asks
mi.timing: Not stated on the pages we read.
mi.renew: Not stated on the pages we read.
mi.call: Michigan Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity (michigan.gov/leo)

hours.14: At most employers the federal limits apply and they are stricter: school days up to 3 hours, school weeks up to 18 hours, non-school days up to 8 hours, 40 a week when school is out, between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. (9 p.m. from June 1 to Labor Day). Michigan's own rules also say not before 7 a.m. or after 9 p.m. for 14 and 15, and no more than 48 hours of school and work combined in a week.
hours.16: Not more than 24 hours in a workweek when school is in session, or 48 when it is not. Not before 6 a.m. or after 10:30 p.m. Sunday to Thursday, and not after 11:30 p.m. Friday and Saturday. These limits come from a state webinar PDF, so confirm with the state.

mi.wage: $13.73 an hour in 2026 and $15.00 from Jan 1, 2027. Workers 16 and 17 may be paid 85 percent.

minAge.note: In general the minimum age for youth employment in Michigan is 14.

job.text: A minor must have a valid work permit before starting work. Michigan's page says the law covers employers of anyone under 18, including volunteers, so ask the program about a volunteer role.

program.text: A paid youth program is a paid job, so the job rule applies. Read the program's own steps for what to turn in.

odd.text: The pages we read do not say whether odd jobs for neighbors need a permit. Ask the Michigan Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity.

own.text: The pages we read do not say whether running your own small business needs a permit. Ask the Michigan Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity.

volunteer.text: The pages we read do not say whether volunteering needs a permit. Ask the Michigan Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity.

intern.text: We found no page here that sets its own internship rule, so the federal fact sheet is the guide: a for-profit generally must pay an intern who is really an employee. Ask a parent or school counselor to check an unpaid one at a business, and ask the Michigan Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity.

family.text: The pages we read do not say about work for a parent's business. Ask the Michigan Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity.

acting.text: The pages we read do not say about acting or modeling. Ask the Michigan Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity.

mi.adult: At 18 you do not need a youth employment permit in Michigan.

nc.name: North Carolina
nc.issuer: The employer starts it in the state's online system. You, a parent or guardian and the employer sign it electronically.
steps: Get a firm job offer first.
Your employer starts the certificate in the state system. You and a parent should not start it.
You, a parent or guardian and the employer sign electronically before your first day.
nc.timing: Not stated on the pages we read.
nc.renew: Not stated on the pages we read.

links.t: US DOL Fact Sheet 32: youth minimum wage

hours.14: No more than 3 hours a day when school is in session or 8 when it is not. No more than 18 hours a week in school weeks or 40 when school is out, and only outside school hours. A 30 minute break after 5 hours in a row. North Carolina adopts the federal limits, so 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. applies (9 p.m. in summer).
hours.16: You cannot work between 11 p.m. and 5 a.m. when there is school the next day, unless a parent and your principal give written permission. The page sets no other daily or weekly cap for 16 and 17.

nc.wage: $7.25 an hour (the page says currently, and gives no year). Under federal law an employer may pay $4.25 to workers under 20 for their first 90 days.

minAge.note: Work is generally not permitted for youths under 14 in North Carolina, with exceptions.

job.text: Youth under 18 who work in North Carolina must have a Youth Employment Certificate.

program.text: A paid youth program is a paid job, so the job rule applies. Read the program's own steps for what to turn in.

odd.text: The pages we read do not say whether odd jobs for neighbors need a permit. Ask the North Carolina Department of Labor.

own.text: The pages we read do not say whether running your own small business needs a permit. Ask the North Carolina Department of Labor.

volunteer.text: The pages we read do not say whether volunteering needs a permit. Ask the North Carolina Department of Labor.

intern.text: We found no page here that sets its own internship rule, so the federal fact sheet is the guide: a for-profit generally must pay an intern who is really an employee. Ask a parent or school counselor to check an unpaid one at a business, and ask the North Carolina Department of Labor.

family.text: The pages we read do not say about work for a parent's business. Ask the North Carolina Department of Labor.

acting.text: The pages we read do not say about acting or modeling. Ask the North Carolina Department of Labor.

nc.adult: At 18 you do not need a Youth Employment Certificate.

nj.name: New Jersey
nj.issuer: The New Jersey Department of Labor, online. Schools are no longer part of the process.
steps: Get the job offer first.
Apply for working papers online with the state, with a parent.
Your employer must register online too.
nj.timing: Not stated on the pages we read.
nj.renew: Not stated on the pages we read.
nj.call: New Jersey Department of Labor and Workforce Development (nj.gov/labor/youngworkers)

links.t: NJ press release on working papers

hours.14: Workers under 16 may not work more than 40 hours a week and 8 hours a day. At most employers the federal limits apply and they are stricter: school days up to 3 hours, school weeks up to 18 hours, non-school days up to 8 hours, 40 a week when school is out, between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. (9 p.m. from June 1 to Labor Day).
hours.16: Workers 16 and up may work up to 50 hours in a week and 10 hours a day only between the last day of school and Labor Day. A school-week limit of about 40 hours a week and 8 hours a day appears in a state page summary, so confirm it. A 30 minute break after 6 hours in a row.

nj.wage: $15.92 an hour in 2026 for most employees, and $16.48 from Jan 1, 2027.

minAge.note: Minors must be at least 14 to work in most jobs in New Jersey, with limited exceptions.

pa.name: Pennsylvania
pa.issuer: A school district issuing officer. You may apply in person or virtually.
steps: Get the job first.
Apply with the issuing officer at your school district.
Under 16, a parent or guardian fills out a written statement that grants permission and acknowledges the duties and hours (Form LLC-75).
bring: Form LLC-75 if you are under 16
pa.timing: Not stated on the pages we read.
pa.renew: The Education Department page says the permit lasts until age 18. That came from a page summary, so confirm.

hours.14: School in session: 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., up to 3 hours on school days and 18 hours a school week. School out: 7 a.m. to 9 p.m., up to 8 hours a day and 40 a week.
hours.16: School in session: 6 a.m. to midnight, up to 8 hours on school days and 28 hours a school week. School out: 6 a.m. to 1 a.m., up to 10 hours a day and 48 a week.

pa.wage: $7.25 an hour. Under federal law an employer may pay $4.25 to workers under 20 for their first 90 days.

minAge.note: Minors under 14 may not work in any occupation, with very limited exceptions such as caddies at 12 and news carriers at 11.

ma.name: Massachusetts
steps: Get the job first.
Apply at the superintendent of schools' office. At 14 or 15, a doctor must fill out the Physician's Certificate of Health part.
Give the permit to your employer.
bring: A doctor's certificate if you are 14 or 15

hours.14: School year: 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. and not during school hours, up to 3 hours a school day and 18 a week. Summer (July 1 to Labor Day): 7 a.m. to 9 p.m., up to 8 hours a day and 40 a week.
hours.16: 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. on school nights, up to 48 hours a week and 9 hours a day. After 8 p.m. an adult must be at the workplace to supervise 14 to 17 year olds.

ma.wage: At least $15.00 an hour under state law. We could not read the current 2026 rate because mass.gov blocked our reader.

bc.name: British Columbia (Canada)
bc.permit: Written parental consent (and a child employment permit for some ages and jobs)
bc.issuer: Your parent or guardian gives written permission. The employer keeps it on file.
steps: A parent or guardian gives written permission for you to work. The employer keeps a record.
You must work under the direct supervision of someone who is at least 19.
Ages 12 to 15 need a permit unless the work is light work such as lifeguard, camp leader, server, cashier or tutor. Ask the Employment Standards Branch.
bring: Written permission from a parent or guardian
bc.timing: Not stated on the pages we read.
bc.renew: Not stated on the pages we read.
bc.call: BC Employment Standards Branch (gov.bc.ca, young people)

hours.14: Children under 15 cannot work during school hours, more than 4 hours on school days, more than 7 hours on a non-school day, more than 20 hours in a week with 5 school days, or more than 35 hours a week when school is not in session.
hours.16: Employers of children 15 or older follow the standard rules for hours of work.

bc.wage: C$18.25 an hour as of June 1, 2026.

minAge.note: Children 12 and 13, and 14 and 15, need a permit unless they do light work only.

job.text: In British Columbia a parent or guardian must give written permission for a child to work, and ages 12 to 15 may need a child employment permit unless the work is light work. Ask the Employment Standards Branch.

program.text: A paid youth program is a paid job, so the job rule applies. Read the program's own steps for what to turn in.

oh.name: Ohio
oh.issuer: Your school issues it, from a form you complete with your employer and a parent.
steps: Get the job first. Complete the pre-application form with your potential employer and your parent or legal guardian.
Take the form to your school. The school issues the permit based on the form.
Ages 16 and 17 need no permit for nonagricultural, nonhazardous work during summer vacation. They need proof of age and a signed parent or guardian consent statement.
bring: A doctor's certificate, if the form asks for one
oh.timing: Not stated on the pages we read.
oh.renew: Not stated on the pages we read.
oh.call: Ohio Department of Commerce, Minor Work Permits (minorworkpermit.com.ohio.gov)

hours.14: Under 16: not before 7 a.m. Not after 9 p.m. from June 1 to Sept 1, or after 7 p.m. at other times (7 to 9 p.m. the night before a non-school day with parent approval). Up to 3 hours on a school day, 18 hours in a school week, 8 hours on a non-school day, 40 hours when school is out. A 30 minute rest after 5 hours in a row. This law took effect Oct 9, 2026.
hours.16: Ages 16 and 17 may not work after 11 p.m. on a night before a school day, or before 7 a.m. on a school day (6 a.m. if not employed after 8 p.m. the night before).

oh.wage: We could not confirm Ohio's 2026 minimum wage because the state's website was down when we checked. Under 16, the employer must pay at least the federal $7.25.

minAge.note: Every minor 14 through 17 needs a working permit under Ohio law. We did not find a Commerce page that states the minimum age outright.

job.text: Every minor 14 through 17 needs a working permit unless Ohio law says otherwise. Ages 16 and 17 need none for nonagricultural, nonhazardous summer-vacation work.

md.name: Maryland
md.issuer: The state: see the Maryland Division of Labor and Industry page for how to apply.
steps: Get the job offer first. Maryland does not issue permits until you are offered a job.
Apply for the work permit through the Maryland Division of Labor and Industry.
Give a copy to your employer before you start.
md.timing: Not stated on the pages we read.
md.renew: Not stated on the pages we read.
md.call: Maryland Division of Labor and Industry (labor.maryland.gov)

hours.14: At most employers the federal limits apply and they are stricter: school days up to 3 hours, school weeks up to 18 hours, non-school days up to 8 hours, 40 a week when school is out, between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. (9 p.m. from June 1 to Labor Day). This matches Maryland's page.
hours.16: Ages 16 and 17 may not spend more than 12 hours in a combination of school and work each day, and must have at least 8 straight hours off from work and school in each 24 hours.

md.wage: $15.00 an hour statewide. Employees under 18 must earn at least 85 percent of the state rate. Prince George's County is $15.30 from July 1, 2026, and Montgomery County is $15.95, $16.50 or $18.00 depending on the employer's size.

minAge.note: Work permits are not issued to minors under the age of 14.

job.text: Work permits are required for all minors under 18 to work in Maryland. They are not issued to minors under 14, and not until a job has been offered.
